3	Our findings are bounded by four limitations.
4	\textbf{Sparsity sweet spot.} 30\% is the lowest-degradation level; at 50\%, all methods collapse on reasoning tasks, and a separate predictor must be retrained per target.
5	\textbf{Knowledge-intensive regression.} KL consistently underperforms on MMLU and GSM8K across scales (8B: $-$5.2pp MMLU; 14B: $-$19.9pp GSM8K), suggesting output-distribution objectives systematically sacrifice reasoning-critical pathways.
6	\textbf{Evaluation scope.} Open-ended generation (e.g., MT-Bench) and contexts beyond 2048 tokens remain untested.
7	\textbf{Baseline coverage.} The 30\% isocompute comparison lacks a BCE 2700-step baseline; WikiText-2 evaluation shares provenance with the training corpus (WikiText-103), partially mitigated by C4 OOD results (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).

\section*{Limitations}

Our findings are bounded by four limitations.
\textbf{Sparsity sweet spot.} 30\% is the lowest-degradation level; at 50\%, all methods collapse on reasoning tasks, and a separate predictor must be retrained per target.
\textbf{Knowledge-intensive regression.} KL consistently underperforms on MMLU and GSM8K across scales (8B: $-$5.2pp MMLU; 14B: $-$19.9pp GSM8K), suggesting output-distribution objectives systematically sacrifice reasoning-critical pathways.
\textbf{Evaluation scope.} Open-ended generation (e.g., MT-Bench) and contexts beyond 2048 tokens remain untested.
\textbf{Baseline coverage.} The 30\% isocompute comparison lacks a BCE 2700-step baseline; WikiText-2 evaluation shares provenance with the training corpus (WikiText-103), partially mitigated by C4 OOD results (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).

Learned sparsity predictors for SwiGLU LLMs predominantly use binary cross-entropy (BCE), training each neuron independently, yet inference allocates budgets globally via top-$k$ ranking.
We train lightweight predictors ($<$1\% of base parameters) with forward KL divergence, coupling all mask decisions through the output distribution.
On LLaMA-3.1-8B at 30\% sparsity, the KL predictor reduces perplexity by 14.5\% over TEAL at matched sparsity, with directional commonsense gains ($n{=}3$) but knowledge-intensive regression (8B MMLU $-$5.2pp, CIs overlap; 14B GSM8K $-$19.9pp, $n{=}3$); post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) becomes redundant.
Output-distribution optimization yields masks that diverge 46--68\% from magnitude-based targets; a target-swap ablation suggests these discovered patterns carry most of the quality information: BCE trained on KL-derived targets approaches KL-level PPL (PPL gap $\leq$0.65pp; 3-seed, 30\%).
Per-layer controls show the signal type gap (9.47 PPL) dwarfs the coupling breadth range (2.08 PPL) at 30\%, though the decomposition is confounded by train--inference mismatch; a $K{=}4$ control suggests task-dependent coupling effects (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Qwen-2.5-14B confirms PPL generalization with scale-dependent downstream effects.
This is primarily an empirical study; wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	How the training objective shapes learned sparsity prediction quality is an open question for SwiGLU LLMs~\cite{shazeer2020glu}. SwiGLU FFN blocks exhibit high contextual sparsity, but their gated activation makes importance prediction challenging: neuron importance depends on both gate and up-projection values, a target that magnitude-based methods handle suboptimally.
4	Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they predominantly rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
5	Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: the TEAL (training-free activation sparsity;~\citealp{liu2025teal}) top-$k$ mechanism ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
6	This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
7	Unlike MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm}, which applies KL to static N:M weight masks, we address contextual activation sparsity where masks must generalize to unseen inputs, vary per token, and coordinate across layers through global allocation.
8	
9	Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
10	KL's coupled gradients discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (mean per-layer Jaccard distance).
11	A target-swap ablation shows KL-discovered mask targets carry most of the quality information: BCE retrained on KL-derived targets approaches KL PPL ($\leq$0.65pp gap, 3-seed), while magnitude-trained BCE yields 28.13$\pm$0.20. Per-layer controls suggest coupling effects are task-dependent, with larger impacts on commonsense than knowledge tasks (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
12	
13	We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
14	At 30\% sparsity under uniform allocation, the predictor reduces TEAL's perplexity by 14.5\% at matched sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30, both at 28.5\%) with downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\% vs.\ 65.3\% dense, 3-seed); global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed variance ($7.3\times$).
15	At 50\%, the perplexity advantage widens (50\% over TEAL), but downstream reasoning collapses regardless of method.
16	
17	Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (3-seed) confirms the PPL advantage ($-$17.3\%) with directional commonsense gains but tied MMLU; preliminary evaluation on Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} shows consistent PPL improvement but reasoning decline (GSM8K $-$19.9pp, $\sigma$=5.3pp; MMLU $-$2.8pp).
18	This paper is primarily an empirical study characterizing how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality across allocation strategies, sparsity levels, and model scales. The central finding---that output-distribution alignment consistently and substantially outperforms per-neuron classification for learned sparsity---is the paper's contribution. Without sparse kernel support, the predictor adds 6.4\% latency overhead; wall-clock speedup is not addressed (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).
19	While individual components (KL divergence, Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation) are established techniques, their application to contextual activation sparsity prediction has not been explored, and the resulting empirical behaviors are non-obvious.
20	
21	Our contributions are:
22	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
23	\item \emph{Empirical:} Output-distribution alignment ranking across five losses, with per-layer decomposition showing the signal type gap (9.47 PPL) dwarfs the coupling breadth range (2.08 PPL), though confounded by train--inference mismatch (\S\ref{sec:perlayer});
24	\item \emph{Empirical:} Cross-scale evidence (7--14B) with task-type split: KL outperforms on PPL and commonsense but shows systematic knowledge regression, structural to output-distribution optimization (C4 control; \S\ref{sec:experiments});
25	\item \emph{Analytical:} Target-swap ablation suggests KL-discovered mask targets transfer to BCE; per-layer controls suggest task-dependent coupling effects (\S\ref{sec:perlayer});
26	\item \emph{Analytical:} KL-derived masks render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:compensation}).
27	\end{itemize}
28	
29	\begin{figure}[t]
30	\centering
31	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_overview.pdf}
32	\caption{Method overview: a lightweight per-layer predictor produces importance scores trained via KL divergence with Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation. At inference, scores feed TEAL's global top-$k$ allocation without compensation networks.}
33	\label{fig:overview}
34	\end{figure}
35

1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	How the training objective shapes learned sparsity prediction quality is an open question for SwiGLU LLMs~\cite{shazeer2020glu}. SwiGLU FFN blocks exhibit high contextual sparsity, but their gated activation makes importance prediction challenging: neuron importance depends on both gate and up-projection values, a target that magnitude-based methods handle suboptimally.
4	Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they predominantly rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
5	Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: the TEAL (training-free activation sparsity;~\citealp{liu2025teal}) top-$k$ mechanism ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
6	This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
7	Unlike MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm}, which applies KL to static N:M weight masks, we address contextual activation sparsity where masks must generalize to unseen inputs, vary per token, and coordinate across layers through global allocation.
8	
9	Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
10	KL's coupled gradients discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (mean per-layer Jaccard distance).
11	A target-swap ablation shows KL-discovered mask targets carry most of the quality information: BCE retrained on KL-derived targets approaches KL PPL ($\leq$0.65pp gap, 3-seed), while magnitude-trained BCE yields 28.13$\pm$0.20. Per-layer controls suggest coupling effects are task-dependent, with larger impacts on commonsense than knowledge tasks (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
12	
13	We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
14	At 30\% sparsity under uniform allocation, the predictor reduces TEAL's perplexity by 14.5\% at matched sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30, both at 28.5\%) with downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\% vs.\ 65.3\% dense, 3-seed); global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed variance ($7.3\times$).
15	At 50\%, the perplexity advantage widens (50\% over TEAL), but downstream reasoning collapses regardless of method.
16	
17	Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (3-seed) confirms the PPL advantage ($-$17.3\%) with directional commonsense gains but tied MMLU; preliminary evaluation on Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} shows consistent PPL improvement but reasoning decline (GSM8K $-$19.9pp, $\sigma$=5.3pp; MMLU $-$2.8pp).
18	This paper is primarily an empirical study characterizing how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality across allocation strategies, sparsity levels, and model scales. The central finding---that output-distribution alignment consistently and substantially outperforms per-neuron classification for learned sparsity---is the paper's contribution. Without sparse kernel support, the predictor adds 6.4\% latency overhead; wall-clock speedup is not addressed (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).
19	While individual components (KL divergence, Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation) are established techniques, their application to contextual activation sparsity prediction has not been explored, and the resulting empirical behaviors are non-obvious.
20	
21	Our contributions are:
22	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
23	\item \emph{Empirical:} Output-distribution alignment ranking across five losses, with per-layer decomposition showing the signal type gap (9.47 PPL) exceeds the coupling breadth range (2.08 PPL), though confounded by train--inference mismatch (\S\ref{sec:perlayer});
24	\item \emph{Empirical:} Cross-scale evidence (7--14B) with task-type split: KL outperforms on PPL and commonsense but shows systematic knowledge regression, structural to output-distribution optimization (C4 control; \S\ref{sec:experiments});
25	\item \emph{Analytical:} Target-swap ablation suggests KL-discovered mask targets transfer to BCE; per-layer controls suggest task-dependent coupling effects (\S\ref{sec:perlayer});
26	\item \emph{Analytical:} KL-derived masks render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:compensation}).
27	\end{itemize}

How the training objective shapes learned sparsity prediction quality is an open question for SwiGLU LLMs~\cite{shazeer2020glu}. SwiGLU FFN blocks exhibit high contextual sparsity, but their gated activation makes importance prediction challenging: neuron importance depends on both gate and up-projection values, a target that magnitude-based methods handle suboptimally.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they predominantly rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: the TEAL (training-free activation sparsity;~\citealp{liu2025teal}) top-$k$ mechanism ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
Unlike MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm}, which applies KL to static N:M weight masks, we address contextual activation sparsity where masks must generalize to unseen inputs, vary per token, and coordinate across layers through global allocation.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
KL's coupled gradients discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (mean per-layer Jaccard distance).
A target-swap ablation shows KL-discovered mask targets carry most of the quality information: BCE retrained on KL-derived targets approaches KL PPL ($\leq$0.65pp gap, 3-seed), while magnitude-trained BCE yields 28.13$\pm$0.20. Per-layer controls suggest coupling effects are task-dependent, with larger impacts on commonsense than knowledge tasks (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
At 30\% sparsity under uniform allocation, the predictor reduces TEAL's perplexity by 14.5\% at matched sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30, both at 28.5\%) with downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\% vs.\ 65.3\% dense, 3-seed); global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed variance ($7.3\times$).
At 50\%, the perplexity advantage widens (50\% over TEAL), but downstream reasoning collapses regardless of method.

Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (3-seed) confirms the PPL advantage ($-$17.3\%) with directional commonsense gains but tied MMLU; preliminary evaluation on Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} shows consistent PPL improvement but reasoning decline (GSM8K $-$19.9pp, $\sigma$=5.3pp; MMLU $-$2.8pp).
This paper is primarily an empirical study characterizing how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality across allocation strategies, sparsity levels, and model scales. The central finding---that output-distribution alignment consistently and substantially outperforms per-neuron classification for learned sparsity---is the paper's contribution. Without sparse kernel support, the predictor adds 6.4\% latency overhead; wall-clock speedup is not addressed (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).
While individual components (KL divergence, Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation) are established techniques, their application to contextual activation sparsity prediction has not been explored, and the resulting empirical behaviors are non-obvious.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{Empirical:} Output-distribution alignment ranking across five losses, with per-layer decomposition showing the signal type gap (9.47 PPL) exceeds the coupling breadth range (2.08 PPL), though confounded by train--inference mismatch (\S\ref{sec:perlayer});
\item \emph{Empirical:} Cross-scale evidence (7--14B) with task-type split: KL outperforms on PPL and commonsense but shows systematic knowledge regression, structural to output-distribution optimization (C4 control; \S\ref{sec:experiments});
\item \emph{Analytical:} Target-swap ablation suggests KL-discovered mask targets transfer to BCE; per-layer controls suggest task-dependent coupling effects (\S\ref{sec:perlayer});
\item \emph{Analytical:} KL-derived masks render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:compensation}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Output-distribution alignment is the primary design dimension for learned sparsity prediction, outperforming BCE and MSE across five losses.
The KL predictor reduces PPL by 14.5\% over TEAL at 30\%, confirmed on Mistral-7B ($-$17.3\%) and Qwen-2.5-14B.
Gains are task-type dependent: KL improves commonsense reasoning but degrades knowledge-intensive tasks (C4 control confirms structural to KL), suggesting KL for commonsense/PPL and TEAL for knowledge tasks.
The signal type gap (9.47 PPL) exceeds the coupling breadth range (2.08 PPL), though the decomposition is confounded by train--inference mismatch (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}); disentangling these factors remains an open question.
Downstream differences are directional ($n{=}3$, CIs overlap). Code released upon acceptance.

Learned sparsity predictors for SwiGLU LLMs predominantly use binary cross-entropy (BCE), training each neuron independently, yet inference allocates budgets globally via top-$k$ ranking.
We train lightweight predictors ($<$1\% of base parameters) with forward KL divergence, coupling all mask decisions through the output distribution.
On LLaMA-3.1-8B at 30\% sparsity, the KL predictor reduces perplexity by 14.5\% over TEAL at matched sparsity, with directional commonsense gains ($n{=}3$) but knowledge-intensive regression (8B MMLU $-$5.2pp, CIs overlap; 14B GSM8K $-$19.9pp, $n{=}3$); post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) becomes redundant.
Output-distribution optimization yields masks that diverge 46--68\% from magnitude-based targets; a target-swap ablation suggests these discovered patterns carry most of the quality information: BCE trained on KL-derived targets approaches KL-level PPL (PPL gap $\leq$0.65pp; 3-seed, 30\%).
Per-layer controls show the signal type gap (9.47 PPL) exceeds the coupling breadth range (2.08 PPL) at 30\%, though the decomposition is confounded by train--inference mismatch; a $K{=}4$ control suggests task-dependent coupling effects (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Qwen-2.5-14B confirms PPL generalization with scale-dependent downstream effects.
This is primarily an empirical study; wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here.

\section*{Limitations}

Our findings are bounded by four limitations.
\textbf{Sparsity sweet spot.} 30\% is the lowest-degradation level; at 50\%, all methods collapse on reasoning tasks, and a separate predictor must be retrained per target.
\textbf{Knowledge-intensive regression.} KL consistently underperforms on MMLU and GSM8K across scales (8B: $-$5.2pp MMLU; 14B: $-$19.9pp GSM8K), suggesting output-distribution objectives systematically sacrifice reasoning-critical pathways.
\textbf{Evaluation scope.} Open-ended generation (e.g., MT-Bench) and contexts beyond 2048 tokens remain untested.
\textbf{Baseline coverage.} The 30\% isocompute comparison lacks a BCE 2700-step baseline; WikiText-2 evaluation shares provenance with the training corpus (WikiText-103), partially mitigated by C4 OOD results (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Training-Free Activation Sparsity.}
TEAL~\cite{liu2025teal} applies global top-$k$ selection by activation magnitude and achieves 40--50\% sparsity with no training cost.
CATS~\cite{lee2024cats} adapts per-layer thresholds for SiLU/SwiGLU activations; R-Sparse~\cite{zhang2025rsparse} predicts sparsity from rank-aware SVD projections; DIP~\cite{federici2025dip} combines dynamic input pruning with cache-aware masking; SparseInfer~\cite{shin2025sparseinfer} and GRASP~\cite{shin2025grasp} predict activation sparsity patterns without additional training.
LaRoSA~\cite{huang2025larosa} applies layerwise orthogonal rotations for structured activation sparsity with wall-clock speedup on SiLU models.
Wang et al.~\cite{wang2025dynamicsparse}, AWQ~\cite{lin2024awq}, and Outlier Suppression+~\cite{wei2023outlier} address sparsity--quantization interactions and activation-aware quantization.
Dhar et al.~\cite{dhar2024activation} characterize activation sparsity opportunities across architectures, showing that SwiGLU models exhibit lower natural sparsity than ReLU counterparts.
OWL~\cite{yin2024owl} determines per-layer sparsity ratios from outlier distributions for weight pruning.
ActTail~\cite{zheng2026acttail} applies heavy-tailed self-regularization for global activation sparsity allocation; WiSparse~\cite{yang2026wisparse} proposes weight-aware mixed activation sparsity.
All training-free methods determine masks from fixed statistics or input-independent criteria, while our predictor generates \emph{input-dependent} masks trained to minimize output-distribution divergence.

\paragraph{Predictor-Based Contextual Sparsity.}
DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} introduced learned sparsity predictors trained via BCE to classify each neuron independently.
ShadowLLM~\cite{akhauri2024shadowllm} uses attention-based routing with per-layer MSE supervision for intermediate coupling within each layer but without end-to-end gradient signal.
FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} adds a 67.2M-parameter compensation network using BCE for mask prediction, adding inference latency.
SVD-CSP~\cite{serbin2026svdcsp} compresses sparsity predictors via SVD decomposition for reduced predictor overhead.
Dhar et al.~\cite{dhar2025clustering} compress activation patterns via clustering for efficient neuron-level prediction.
LazyLLM~\cite{fu2024lazyllm} dynamically prunes tokens across layers for long-context efficiency; COTS~\cite{zhang2025cots} exploits connected activation patterns for structured sparse inference.
PowerInfer~\cite{song2024powerinfer} and PowerInfer-2~\cite{xue2024powerinfer2} exploit power-law activation frequencies for GPU--CPU/NPU scheduling.
MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} shares the recipe-level principle of frozen weights + learnable masks + KL training.
The methods differ in three respects: (a) MaskLLM's mask parameters are fixed per input (static N:M weight sparsity via Gumbel-Softmax), while our predictor generates \emph{per-token} masks that must generalize to unseen inputs; (b) static N:M patterns have no cross-layer allocation interaction, whereas our masks coordinate through TEAL's global top-$k$; (c) activation masks must be robust to distribution shift at inference, while weight masks are input-independent.
Our contribution beyond the shared recipe is analytical: a systematic decomposition of signal type vs.\ coupling scope for sparsity prediction training, via target-swap ablation and per-layer KL controls (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
All prior predictor-based methods for activation sparsity use decomposed (BCE) or intermediate (MSE) objectives where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
We empirically observe that an output-distribution-coupled objective propagates gradients through all downstream layers and quantify when this matters for global allocation quality.

\paragraph{Static Bias Correction.}
SPON (Spontaneous Neurons;~\citealp{xu2025spon}) learns input-independent bias vectors via closed-form KL minimization per layer, absorbed into weights at deployment.
Our method is fundamentally different: a per-token contextual predictor trained end-to-end across all layers that produces input-dependent masks.
SPON solves a static per-layer problem; we solve a global dynamic prediction problem. The two are weakly correlated (cosine similarity 0.196, $R^2$=0.038; \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\paragraph{Activation Function Engineering.}
ReLU Strikes Back~\cite{mirzadeh2024relu} replaces SiLU with ReLU for $>$90\% natural sparsity; TurboSparse~\cite{song2024turbosparse} and ProSparse~\cite{song2025prosparse} engineer extreme sparsity through activation modifications; the Sparsing Law~\cite{luo2024sparsinglaw} formalizes how activation density increases with training compute.
MiniTron~\cite{muralidharan2024minitron} combines structured pruning with distillation but modifies architecture permanently.
Haziza et al.~\cite{haziza2025accelerating} demonstrate 2:4 semi-structured activation sparsity with hardware-native acceleration, complementing our unstructured approach.
MoC~\cite{wu2025moc} selectively activates Top-$K$ FFN channels using SwiGLU's native gating during pretraining.
All require retraining or weight modification; our method is a plug-in predictor on \emph{unmodified} SwiGLU models.

\paragraph{Weight Pruning, Distillation, and Routing.}
Wanda~\cite{sun2024wanda}, SparseGPT~\cite{frantar2023sparsegpt}, and SliceGPT~\cite{ashkboos2024slicegpt} produce static weight masks via one-shot or structured pruning; Polar Sparsity~\cite{shrestha2025polar} scales contextual sparsity to batched inference by shifting focus from MLP to attention head sparsity; Alizadeh et al.~\cite{alizadeh2024llmflash} leverage activation sparsity for memory-efficient inference via selective flash loading.
Switch Transformers~\cite{fedus2022switch} and Mixture-of-Depths~\cite{raposo2024mod} achieve conditional computation through learned routing.
KL-based distillation~\cite{kim2016sequencekd,sanh2019distilbert,gu2024minillm,agarwal2024gkd,ko2024distillm} trains compact students; SparseLoRA~\cite{khaki2025sparselora} exploits contextual sparsity for fine-tuning.
We apply the KL principle to train a sparsity predictor on unmodified dense models, using Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling~\cite{maddison2017concrete,louizos2018l0} for differentiable discrete mask optimization.

\paragraph{MoE Routing and Gated Sparsity.}
Expert Choice routing~\cite{zhou2022expertchoice} lets each expert select its top-$k$ tokens under a fixed capacity budget, a global allocation perspective that parallels TEAL's neuron-level global top-$k$.
D2D-MoE~\cite{szatkowski2024d2dmoe} converts dense SwiGLU layers into dynamic-$k$ MoE by exploiting the same activation sparsity we target, but restructures the network into discrete experts rather than predicting masks on the original architecture.
MoNE~\cite{cheng2025mone} applies neuron-granular top-$k$ selection within each MoE expert during pretraining for fine-grained conditional computation without additional routing parameters.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	
6	\paragraph{Model and Predictor.}
7	We evaluate on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}, which uses SwiGLU FFN blocks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} with $d_{\text{model}}=4096$ and $d_{\text{ff}}=14336$ across 32 layers.
8	The sparsity predictor is a two-layer MLP with 2.37M parameters per layer (75.9M total), implemented as Linear($4096 \to 128$) + GELU + Linear($128 \to 14336$), trained to produce per-neuron importance scores that minimize output-distribution divergence under sparsity.
9	
10	\paragraph{Training.}
11	All predictors are trained for 1000 steps on WikiText-103 with sequence length 2048 and batch size 4 on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (96\,GB), using AdamW~\cite{loshchilov2019adamw} with learning rate $1 \times 10^{-3}$, weight decay $1 \times 10^{-2}$, and cosine decay.
12	The KL predictor uses Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} with temperature $\tau=1.0$ annealed to $0.1$ over training.
13	
14	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
15	We report perplexity on WikiText-2~\cite{merity2017pointer} (seq\_len=2048) and downstream accuracy on ARC-Challenge (25-shot), WinoGrande (5-shot), MMLU (5-shot), GSM8K (8-shot), HellaSwag (10-shot), and PIQA (0-shot).
16	
17	\paragraph{Inference Protocol.}
18	At inference, the predictor produces per-neuron scores that are passed to TEAL's global top-$k$ allocation mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal}, which distributes the sparsity budget across layers non-uniformly.
19	We term this \textit{predictor-TEAL}: the predictor replaces TEAL's magnitude-based scoring while retaining its allocation strategy.
20	
21	\paragraph{Baselines.}
22	We compare against: (1) \textbf{Vanilla TEAL}~\cite{liu2025teal}, which uses activation magnitudes directly\footnote{TEAL is deterministic; single-run evaluation suffices. KL/BCE predictors require multi-seed evaluation due to random initialization.}; (2) \textbf{BCE predictor} (DejaVu-style~\cite{liu2023dejavu}), trained with per-neuron binary cross-entropy on magnitude-based oracle masks for 1000 and 2700 steps; and (3) \textbf{Uniform allocation}, which distributes the sparsity budget equally across layers.
23	
24	
25	\subsection{Main Results}
26	
27	Table~\ref{tab:main} presents the primary comparison. Uniform allocation preserves downstream performance best; global allocation is analyzed to understand allocation-quality tradeoffs (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
28	At 30\% sparsity, output-distribution KL under uniform allocation achieves PPL 8.81$\pm$0.02 (3-seed), a 14.5\% reduction over TEAL at matched actual sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30, both at 28.5\%; Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
29	Uniform allocation yields stable downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed; Appendix~\ref{app:stability}), while global top-$k$ exhibits high seed variance (35.7$\pm$9.5\%) from late-layer starvation (L31 retention 28.4\%; \S\ref{sec:scaling}). % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform, kl30_s123_uniform, kl30_s456_uniform, kl30_3seed
30	
31	\paragraph{Task-Type Split.}
32	KL shows directional improvements over TEAL on commonsense reasoning (ARC-c, WG, HellaSwag, PIQA: 4/4 wins at 30\% uniform) but underperforms on knowledge-intensive tasks (MMLU, GSM8K: 0/2).
33	With only three seeds, 95\% confidence intervals for individual downstream tasks overlap; we therefore treat PPL ($\sigma{=}0.02$, non-overlapping) as the primary metric and downstream differences as directional evidence.
34	The KL predictor protects L14--L18 (14--18\% sparsity vs.\ 32\% global mean) while aggressively pruning L22--L28 (48--57\%). Constraint interventions (Appendix~\ref{app:constraint}) confirm a task-dependent trade-off: removing the valley improves MMLU +3.4pp but reduces ARC-c by 1.5pp, consistent with localized factual associations~\cite{geva2023dissecting}; task-aware allocation may resolve this. % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform, teal30_uniform, hellaswag_piqa_kl30_uniform, perlayer_sparsity_analysis, constraint_protect_late, constraint_remove_valley
35	
36	\paragraph{Knowledge-Task Regression: Hypothesis.}
37	Constraint experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:constraint}) confirm allocation contributes: removing the learned valley improves MMLU +3.4pp and GSM8K +1.6pp. A C4-trained control (Appendix~\ref{app:c4_control}) does not alleviate the regression (MMLU 40.0\%, GSM8K 4.1\% vs.\ 40.7\%, 7.5\%), confirming the deficit is structural to forward KL's mode-covering property~\cite{meng2022locating} rather than training data composition. % exp_id: constraint_remove_valley, c4_control_eval
38	
39	At 50\%, the PPL advantage widens (11.92 vs.\ 23.90, 50\% reduction) and generalizes to C4 (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}), but all methods collapse to near-random on MMLU and GSM8K ($\leq$2.7\%); no allocation strategy recovers at this capacity limit. % exp_id: bench_kl50_global, kl50_global_s123_downstream_v2, kl50_global_s456_eval, d030_kl50_uniform, multi_seed_kl50_global
40	
41	\begin{table}[t]
42	\centering
43	\caption{Main results on LLaMA-3.1-8B. $^\ast$$2.71\times$ KL compute (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}). $\pm$: 3-seed; unmarked: s42. $^\ddagger$Actual sparsity: KL 28.5\% vs.\ TEAL 29.3\% at 30\% (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).}
44	\label{tab:main}
45	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
46	\begin{tabular}{llccccc}
47	\toprule
48	Sparsity & Method & PPL$\downarrow$ & ARC-c & WG & MMLU & GSM8K \\
49	\midrule
50	0\% & Dense & 6.12 & 58.28 & 78.06 & 65.27 & 48.75 \\
51	\midrule
52	\multirow{6}{*}{30\%}
53	& TEAL uniform & 10.82 & 39.33 & 65.04 & \textbf{45.86} & \textbf{8.79} \\ % exp_id: teal30_uniform
54	& BCE global & 11.25 & 41.2 & 66.0 & 36.3 & 6.0 \\ % exp_id: bce30_teal_global
55	& BCE uniform & 15.09$\pm$0.13 & 33.45 & 61.09 & 43.05 & 3.97 \\ % exp_id: bce_iso_v3_s42, bce_iso_v3_s123, bce_iso_v3_s456
56	& MSE uniform & 18.52$\pm$1.68 & 35.8$\pm$4.1 & 59.8$\pm$2.6 & 30.7$\pm$2.6 & 2.3$\pm$0.7 \\ % exp_id: mse30_3seed
57	& KL global (Ours)$^\ddagger$ & 8.96$\pm$0.02 & \textbf{43.8$\pm$3.6} & \textbf{70.2$\pm$0.9} & 35.7$\pm$9.5 & 8.0$\pm$0.7 \\ % exp_id: kl30_3seed_global
58	& KL uniform$^\ddagger$ & \textbf{8.81$\pm$0.02} & 43.7$\pm$2.5 & 68.9$\pm$0.4 & 40.7$\pm$1.3 & 7.5$\pm$0.1 \\ % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform, kl30_s123_uniform, kl30_s456_uniform
59	\midrule
60	\multirow{5}{*}{50\%}
61	& TEAL uniform & 23.90 & 27.47 & 54.38 & \textbf{29.26} & 1.74 \\ % exp_id: teal50_uniform
62	& BCE (2700 steps)$^\ast$ & 28.13$\pm$0.20 & 27.6$\pm$0.6 & 51.8$\pm$0.6 & 26.1$\pm$0.5 & 2.1$\pm$0.2 \\ % exp_id: bce50_3seed
63	& MSE uniform & 229.26 & 25.00 & 50.59 & 23.79 & 1.59 \\ % exp_id: mse50_uniform_s42
64	& KL global (Ours) & \textbf{11.84$\pm$0.15} & \textbf{36.3$\pm$3.2} & \textbf{63.8$\pm$0.3} & 28.3$\pm$0.7 & \textbf{2.7$\pm$1.3} \\ % exp_id: bench_kl50_global (s42), kl50_global_s123_reeval (s123 PPL), kl50_global_s123_downstream_v2 (s123 downstream), kl50_global_s456_eval (s456)
65	& KL uniform & 11.92$\pm$0.07 & 33.8$\pm$1.2 & 62.9$\pm$0.1 & 28.0$\pm$0.6 & 2.2$\pm$0.1 \\ % exp_id: bench_kl50_uniform, bench_kl50_uniform_s123, bench_kl50_uniform_s456
66	\bottomrule
67	\end{tabular}}
68	\end{table}
69	
70	
71	\subsection{Extended Training Analysis}
72	\label{sec:isocompute}
73	
74	At $2.71\times$ KL compute budget (2700 steps, matched wall-clock), BCE achieves PPL 28.13$\pm$0.20 (3-seed), still $2.39\times$ worse than KL (11.79). % exp_id: bce50_3seed
75	The gap is systematic: BCE reaches higher oracle F1 (0.613 vs.\ 0.540) with 139\% worse PPL, confirming KL optimizes for distributional fidelity rather than magnitude agreement. % exp_id: f1_oracle_analysis, bce_isocompute_s42
76	
77	
78	\subsection{Mask Pattern Analysis}
79	\label{sec:mask_analysis}
80	
81	KL-derived masks diverge from magnitude oracles: per-layer Jaccard distance averages 68\% at 50\% (64 samples, 131K tokens; Figure~\ref{fig:mask_heatmap}), with cross-seed variation (36.3\%) confirming systematic divergence (Appendices~\ref{app:cross_seed_jaccard},~\ref{app:mask_viz}).
82	Despite this, KL achieves PPL 11.79 vs.\ BCE's 28.13$\pm$0.20, confirming that distributional fidelity, not magnitude agreement, produces better masks. % exp_id: bench_kl50_global, bce50_3seed, c1_mask_overlap
83	Divergence follows a U-shaped per-layer pattern, peaking in late layers (0.70--0.75 at 50\%). % exp_id: c1_mask_overlap
84	
85	\paragraph{Target-Swap Ablation: Target Quality vs.\ Gradient Coupling.}
86	To disentangle whether KL's advantage stems from its coupled gradient pathway or from the mask patterns it discovers, we train a standard BCE predictor on KL-derived oracle masks instead of magnitude-based masks (C1 target-swap ablation).
87	Table~\ref{tab:c1} reports results under TEAL uniform allocation at matched sparsity.
88	
89	\begin{table}[t]
90	\centering
91	\caption{Target-swap ablation (C1): BCE on KL-derived masks vs.\ KL predictor (same seed), TEAL uniform. All seeds show max $\Delta$$\leq$1.70pp at 30\%; max $\Delta$$\leq$0.79pp at 50\% (s42). $^\dagger$\textbf{Provenance:} s42 oracle extracted from an earlier training run (not seed-matched); s123/s456 use seed-matched retrained oracles (Appendix~\ref{app:oracle_provenance}).}
92	\label{tab:c1}
93	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
94	\begin{tabular}{lllccccc}
95	\toprule
96	Sparsity & Seed & Method & PPL$\downarrow$ & ARC-c & WG & MMLU & GSM8K \\
97	\midrule
98	\multirow{6}{*}{30\%}
99	& s42$^\dagger$ & C1 & 9.45 & 40.27 & 67.40 & \textbf{42.30} & \textbf{7.58} \\ % exp_id: c1_ablation_30pct_s42_eval_v2
100	& & KL & \textbf{8.82} & \textbf{40.78} & \textbf{68.59} & 40.6 & 7.35 \\ % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform
101	& s123 & C1 & 8.84 & 44.71 & \textbf{69.77} & \textbf{39.92} & 6.82 \\ % exp_id: eval_c1_retrain_30pct_s123
102	& & KL & \textbf{8.83} & \textbf{45.31} & 69.38 & 39.4 & \textbf{7.51} \\ % exp_id: kl30_s123_eval
103	& s456 & C1 & 8.82 & 44.71 & \textbf{69.93} & 41.04 & 6.60 \\ % exp_id: eval_c1_retrain_30pct_s456
104	& & KL & \textbf{8.79} & \textbf{45.05} & 68.75 & \textbf{42.0} & \textbf{7.58} \\ % exp_id: kl30_s456_uniform_eval
105	\midrule
106	\multirow{2}{*}{50\%}
107	& s42 & C1 & 11.96 & 32.17 & \textbf{63.14} & 27.79 & \textbf{2.05} \\ % exp_id: c1_bce_kl_targets_teal50u
108	& & KL & 11.96 & \textbf{32.59} & 62.35 & \textbf{27.92} & 1.97 \\ % exp_id: c1_kl_teal50u
109	\bottomrule
110	\end{tabular}}
111	\end{table}
112	
113	At 50\% (s42, earlier oracle), C1 matches KL within 0.79pp, while magnitude-trained BCE yields $2.4\times$ worse PPL (Table~\ref{tab:main}).
114	At 30\%, retrained seeds show $\leq$1.18pp agreement\footnote{s42 oracle from earlier checkpoint (gap 0.65pp); s123/s456 use seed-matched converged oracles ($\leq$0.03pp gap).}.
115	C1 demonstrates that KL-discovered mask patterns \emph{transfer} to a simpler training mechanism (PPL within 0.79pp; downstream variation up to 4.5pp MMLU); per-layer KL controls (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}) further suggest task-dependent coupling effects.
116	However, C1 also changes mask representation: binarizing oracle soft logits ($>$0) into hard masks discards ranking information, so the near-zero delta reflects transferability of binary mask \emph{patterns} rather than full predictor knowledge. BCE+Gumbel (32.22) underperforms standard BCE (27.97), indicating trajectory-dependent confounds that prevent clean isolation of target quality from gradient coupling (Appendix~\ref{app:oracle_provenance}). % exp_id: bce50_3seed, c1_bce_kl_targets_30u, c1_s123, bce_gumbel_no_penalty_s42, eval_bce_v3_s42
117	
118	\subsection{Ablation Studies}
119	
120	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} isolates the contribution of each design choice at 30\% and 50\% sparsity.

Looking more carefully at the evaluation protocols, I realize the -17.3% figure refers to the KL PPL improvement versus the TEAL baseline PPL of 8.3807, not a comparison across the three seeds themselves.

Let me work through the actual numbers: if KL PPL is 17.3% lower than TEAL, that gives me roughly 6.929. But when I look at the individual seed results—s42 with a global allocation KL value around 6.7733, s123 showing 7.1491, and s456 at 6.8752—they're using different field names and allocation methods, which makes it hard to know if I'm comparing the right metrics.

I need to search the full registry more systematically to find the consistent TEAL measurements across all seeds and check what the Qwen results look like too.

[System 触发审查]:
R29 审稿报告独立评估请求。DDL 明天 (2026-05-25)，请评估我的 Action Matrix 是否遗漏、方案是否可行。

## R29 审稿概要
Overall: 3.0 (Findings)。3 Critical + 6 Warning + 3 Nice-to-Have。

## 复发问题分析（从 review_issues.yaml）
- W1 (§4.5 confound): 复发 × 10 轮。历轮用 framing 降级（exploratory, observation-first, explicit confound）——每轮仍被 flag。
- W2 (知识退化机制): 复发 × 11 轮。历轮用 C4 control + constraint analysis + task-type split elevation——每轮仍被 flag。
- W3 (统计可靠性): 复发 × 6 轮。历轮加 directional qualifiers——每轮仍被 flag（因 abstract/conclusion 仍报具体数值）。

## 逐条 Action Matrix

### Critical — Evidence Problems（写作已无法实质解决）

**W1: §4.5 confound [复发 × 10 轮, Evidence]**
- 写作手段已用尽 10 轮，仍无法解决结构性 confound
- Q3 提到的 "0.47 PPL" 是 reviewer 误读，paper 实际是 "9.47 PPL"（conclusion L7, abstract L5 已验证）
- 新方案区别于历轮：不再改 framing 语气，而是**结构性压缩** — §4.5 当前主文约 5 行文字 + 1 个 figure，已相当紧凑。进一步压缩空间有限
- 评估：§4.5 的 claim 已降级到 "exploratory observation + explicit confound"，篇幅也合理（~5 行 + figure）。继续压缩可能得不偿失。**建议接受为结构性限制**
- DDL 前可做：无实质性新修改。如果 Reviewer 你认为可以再改什么，请具体建议

**W2: 知识退化机制 [复发 × 11 轮, Evidence]**
- "mode-covering" vs "allocation-induced" 两个解释并存但有张力
- 无法在 DDL 前做 neuron-level attribution 或新实验
- 新方案：在 §4.2 中添加 1-2 句话明确承认两种解释的张力："C4 control rules out training-data bias, but remove-valley and K=4 results suggest allocation patterns contribute alongside any loss-inherent effect; disentangling these factors requires neuron-level attribution beyond our scope."
- 区别于历轮：不再试图用单一解释统一叙事，改为明确声明两因素共存+开放问题

**W3: 统计可靠性 [复发 × 6 轮, Evidence → partially Writing]**
- PPL claims 稳健（σ=0.02），downstream claims 不稳健（MMLU σ=9.5pp）
- 历轮加了 "directional (n=3)" 但 abstract/conclusion 仍报具体 gap 数值
- 新方案（更激进，区别于历轮）：Abstract 和 Conclusion 中的 downstream claims 只保留方向性描述，**删除具体 pp 数值**
  - Abstract L3: "knowledge-intensive regression (8B MMLU −5.2pp, CIs overlap; 14B GSM8K −19.9pp, n=3)" → "knowledge-intensive regression across scales (CIs overlap, n=3; §4.2)"
  - Conclusion L6: 已有方向性描述，但可进一步精简
  - Introduction L17 保留具体数值（正文 with full context）
- 这解决了"abstract/conclusion 报具体数值但统计无意义"的核心矛盾

### Warning — 可执行

**W4: 方法新颖性 [复发 × 4 轮]**
- R1/R2 分歧未解决。当前 "empirical study" 定位正确
- 方案：不做修改。Reviewer 分歧无法通过单方面修改解决

**W5: MSE lr sweep [NEW, Evidence]**
- DDL 前无法做实验
- 方案：在 §4.1 或 Limitations 加一句 caveat："MSE uses identical hyperparameters to KL; its gradient magnitude is ~5× larger, and performance may improve with a dedicated learning rate."

**W6: BCE+Gumbel synergy [NEW, Writing]**
- Actionable。BCE+Gumbel(32.22) vs BCE(27.97) 揭示 Gumbel 对 BCE 有害
- 方案：在 §4.4 添加 1-2 句讨论："Notably, Gumbel relaxation harms BCE (32.22 vs 27.97 PPL), suggesting the benefit of differentiable relaxation depends on loss structure: KL's coupled gradients exploit Gumbel's continuous exploration, while BCE's per-neuron gradients do not."

**W7: STE undershoot [NEW, Evidence]**

覆盖看起来完整。无遗漏。W7 (STE undershoot) 的处理方案合理——ablation table 的脚注 ‡ 已注明 "20.8% actual sparsity at 30% target"，补一句 caveat 即可。

## Q2: W1/W2 "接受为结构性限制" 是否合理？

**W1 (§4.5 confound): 同意接受。** §4.5 当前状态已到位：
- 标题含 "Empirical"
- 正文明确写 "the decomposition is confounded by train–inference mismatch"
- 结论重复 "confounded" + "open question"
- 10 轮 framing 调整已穷尽写作空间。继续改只会引入新的 oscillation 问题（如 R28→R29 反复改 label）

**W2 (知识退化机制): 基本同意，但你提议的补充文字有一个逻辑问题。** §4.2 L37 当前写的是："confirming the deficit is structural to forward KL's mode-covering property rather than training data composition"。这个 "confirming" 语气过强——C4 control 只排除了 training data bias，并没有 confirm mode-covering 是唯一原因。你提议的新句子（"allocation patterns contribute alongside any loss-inherent effect"）与前文 "confirming structural to KL" 形成矛盾。

**建议**：先把 L37 的 "confirming" 弱化为 "suggesting"，然后再加你的张力声明。完整修改：
> "A C4-trained control does not alleviate the regression, suggesting the deficit is structural to the optimization objective rather than training data composition. However, constraint experiments show allocation contributes (MMLU +3.4pp when valley removed), indicating both loss-inherent and allocation-induced factors; disentangling these requires neuron-level attribution beyond our scope."

这需要把 L34 的 constraint results 和 L37 的 C4 control 重新编排，总共 ~20 行文字的 restructure。

## Q3: W3 去掉 abstract 具体 pp 数值是否过度？

**是的，过度了。不建议删除。**

理由：
1. **这些 gap 统计上可能 IS significant**。8B MMLU: gap=-5.2pp, σ_KL=1.3, TEAL 确定性 → 单样本 t = 5.2/(1.3/√3) ≈ 6.9, p<0.01。14B GSM8K: gap=-19.9pp, σ=5.3 → t = 19.9/(5.3/√3) ≈ 6.5, p<0.01。"CIs overlap" 的说法反而值得再审视。
2. 删掉具体数值会让 abstract 变空洞——reviewer 看到 "regression across scales" 会立刻问 "多大?"，反而增加疑虑。
3. 当前 abstract 已有充分 qualifier ("CIs overlap", "n=3")。Reviewer 的 complaint 是关于 n=3 的实验设计，不是关于 abstract 是否报数字。

**替代建议**：保持当前 abstract 文字不变。如果一定要改，只做微调：把 "CIs overlap" 改为 "directional at $n{=}3$" 更准确（因为严格来说 MMLU uniform 的 CI 并不 overlap with TEAL）。

## Q4: C3/C4 全改 "Empirical" 是否缺乏区分度？

**是的，4 个全是 Empirical 确实缺乏区分。** 但 "Analytical" 在 *ACL 语境确实暗示形式化分析/理论推导，C3/C4 不是。R28 从 "Practical" 改 "Analytical"，R29 又说 "Analytical" 不对——label oscillation 正是问题所在。

**建议**：
- C3 → **Diagnostic**: Target-swap ablation 是诊断性实验，用来分析 WHERE the improvement comes from
- C4 → **Practical**: 补偿网络冗余是一个实用发现

最终：C1 Empirical, C2 Empirical, C3 Diagnostic, C4 Practical。每个标签语义清晰，不会再被误读。

## Q5: 其他低成本高收益修改？

**一个小问题**：Abstract 中 "CIs overlap" 可能有误导。实际验算：
- 8B MMLU: KL 40.7±1.3 的 95% CI ≈ [39.0, 42.4]，不与 TEAL 45.86 重叠
- 14B GSM8K: KL 32.2±5.3 的 95% CI ≈ [19.0, 45.4]，不与 TEAL 52.1 重叠

"CIs overlap" 可能指的是 global allocation (MMLU 35.7±9.5) 而非 uniform。但 abstract 报的 -5.2pp 是 uniform 的 gap。建议改为 "directional at $n{=}3$" 或 "CIs wide at $n{=}3$"，避免被审稿人发现不一致。这是 ~5min 修改。

---

## 修改优先级排序（考虑 DDL 压力）

| 优先级 | 修改 | 时间 | 收益 |
|--------|------|------|------|
| P0 | C3/C4 labels → Diagnostic/Practical | 5min | 消除 oscillation |
| P0 | §4.2 "confirming" → "suggesting" + 张力声明 | 20min | W2 结构性改善 |
| P1 | §4.4 BCE+Gumbel synergy 讨论 | 15min | W6 新发现，有说服力 |
| P1 | Abstract "CIs overlap" → "directional at n=3" | 5min | 修正潜在不一致 |
| P2 | MSE hyperparameter caveat | 10min | W5 防御 |
| P2 | Page 20 空白 | 10min | 视觉 |
| P3 | STE caveat | 5min | W7 防御，footnote 已部分覆盖 |

总计约 70min。W1 和 W3 不做修改。

Learned sparsity predictors for SwiGLU LLMs predominantly use binary cross-entropy (BCE), training each neuron independently, yet inference allocates budgets globally via top-$k$ ranking.
We train lightweight predictors ($<$1\% of base parameters) with forward KL divergence, coupling all mask decisions through the output distribution.
On LLaMA-3.1-8B at 30\% sparsity, the KL predictor reduces perplexity by 14.5\% over TEAL at matched sparsity, with directional commonsense gains ($n{=}3$) but knowledge-intensive regression (8B MMLU $-$5.2pp; 14B GSM8K $-$19.9pp; directional at $n{=}3$); post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) becomes redundant.
Output-distribution optimization yields masks that diverge 46--68\% from magnitude-based targets; a target-swap ablation suggests these discovered patterns carry most of the quality information: BCE trained on KL-derived targets approaches KL-level PPL (PPL gap $\leq$0.65pp; 3-seed, 30\%).
Per-layer controls show the signal type gap (9.47 PPL) exceeds the coupling breadth range (2.08 PPL) at 30\%, though the decomposition is confounded by train--inference mismatch; a $K{=}4$ control suggests task-dependent coupling effects (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Qwen-2.5-14B confirms PPL generalization with scale-dependent downstream effects.
This is primarily an empirical study; wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Output-distribution alignment is the primary design dimension for learned sparsity prediction, outperforming BCE and MSE across five losses.
The KL predictor reduces PPL by 14.5\% over TEAL at 30\%, confirmed on Mistral-7B ($-$17.3\%) and Qwen-2.5-14B.
Gains are task-type dependent: KL improves commonsense reasoning but degrades knowledge-intensive tasks (C4 control suggests structural to the optimization objective), suggesting KL for commonsense/PPL and TEAL for knowledge tasks.
The signal type gap (9.47 PPL) exceeds the coupling breadth range (2.08 PPL), though confounded by train--inference mismatch (\S\ref{sec:perlayer}).
Downstream differences are directional ($n{=}3$); code released upon acceptance.
